# Notes on a quiet desk

A desk is a **promise** you make to yourself in the morning and break by lunch. I keep mine *almost* empty: a lamp, a pencil, and the page.

The rule is simple. If a thing does not help the sentence in front of me, it goes in the drawer.

## What stays

- A pencil with a **soft** lead
- A notebook I do not have to finish
- One cup of coffee, *never* two

> Clear the desk and the page clears with it.

Most of what I write starts as a list. The list turns into a paragraph when one item refuses to stay short. That is the item worth writing about, and it is never the one I expected.

## What goes

The phone goes first. Then the second monitor, then the tab with the [style guide](https://example.com/style) I swear I will read. A `todo.md` file can stay, as long as it stays closed.

Some days the drawer wins. I open it for a ruler and come back an hour later with a box of old letters and no new words. On those days I write about the letters.

### A small habit

Before I stop for the day I write one sentence for tomorrow. It does not have to be good. It has to be **there**, so the morning starts in the middle of something instead of at the top of a blank page.

The habit took a month to stick. It stuck because it was small enough to do on a bad day, and a bad day is the only day a habit has to survive.

## Why it matters

A clean desk is not about the desk. It is about the *one* decision it removes: what to look at. With that decision gone, there is only the page, and the page is enough.

I have tried the other way. A desk full of tools feels productive for about ten minutes, then every tool asks for a little attention and the sentence gets none.

So the lamp stays, the pencil stays, and everything else waits in the drawer. The drawer is patient. The sentence is not.

## Afterword

If you try this, start with one thing. Take it off the desk for a week and see if you miss it. Most weeks you will not, and that is the whole lesson.

The last line stays where it is.
